blocks.prompt: 16. If the \(p^{\text{th}}\) term of an A.P. is \(q\) and the \(q^{\text{th}}\) term is \(p\), prove that its \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is \((p + q - n)\).
blocks.explanation:
A proof with letters instead of numbers, but the same idea as Question 10.
Two given terms give two equations for \(a_1\) and \(d\); then we build \(a_n\).
Plan: write both equations, subtract to find \(d\), find \(a_1\), substitute in \(a_n\).
steps:
Given: \(a_p = q,\ a_q = p\) (with \(p \ne q\))
To prove: \(a_n = p + q - n\).
Method: \(a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d\).

Write the two equations
\[a_1 + (p - 1)d = q \quad (1)\]
\[a_1 + (q - 1)d = p \quad (2)\]
Why: The general term with \(n = p\) and \(n = q\).

Subtract to find \(d\)
\[(1) - (2):\ (p - q)d = q - p\]
\[d = \dfrac{q - p}{p - q} = -1\]
Why: \((p - 1) - (q - 1) = p - q\). Since \(p \ne q\) we may divide, and \(q - p = -(p - q)\).

Check
\[a_p = p + q - p = q \;\checkmark\]
\[a_q = p + q - q = p \;\checkmark\]
Why: The formula gives back both given terms.
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is \(p + q - n\).
